questions.q: Find the critical point(s) of $f(x,y)=x^2+3y^2-4x+6y$.
questions.answer: $f_x=2x-4=0 \Rightarrow x=2$. $f_y=6y+6=0 \Rightarrow y=-1$. Critical point: $(2,-1)$.

questions.q: Find the critical point(s) of $f(x,y)=xy-x^2-y^2$.
questions.answer: $f_x=y-2x=0 \Rightarrow y=2x$. $f_y=x-2y=0 \Rightarrow x=2y$. Substituting: $x=2(2x)=4x \Rightarrow x=0$, so $y=0$. Critical point: $(0,0)$.

questions.q: Find the critical point(s) of $f(x,y)=x^3-3xy+y^3$.
questions.answer: $f_x=3x^2-3y=0 \Rightarrow y=x^2$. $f_y=-3x+3y^2=0 \Rightarrow x=y^2$. Substituting $y=x^2$ into $x=y^2$: $x=x^4 \Rightarrow x^4-x=0 \Rightarrow x(x^3-1)=0 \Rightarrow x=0$ or $x=1$. Critical points: $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$.

sections.heading: The Hessian and the Second Derivative Test

questions.q: Classify the critical point $(2,-1)$ of $f(x,y)=x^2+3y^2-4x+6y$ using $D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-(f_{xy})^2$.
Classify the critical point $(0,0)$ of $f(x,y)=xy-x^2-y^2$.
Classify the critical point of $f(x,y)=x^2-y^2$.
Classify both critical points $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ of $f(x,y)=x^3-3xy+y^3$ (found above).

sections.heading: When the Second Derivative Test fails

questions.q: Show that the Second Derivative Test is inconclusive at the critical point $(0,0)$ of $f(x,y)=x^4+y^4$.
questions.answer: $f_x=4x^3$, $f_y=4y^3$, both zero at $(0,0)$. $f_{xx}=12x^2$, $f_{yy}=12y^2$, $f_{xy}=0$, all zero at $(0,0)$, so $D=0$ — the test gives no information.

questions.q: Determine directly (without the Second Derivative Test) whether $(0,0)$ is a local min, max, or saddle for $f(x,y)=x^4+y^4$.
questions.answer: Since $x^4\geq0$ and $y^4\geq0$ for all $(x,y)$, $f(x,y)\geq0=f(0,0)$ everywhere, so $(0,0)$ is a (global, hence local) minimum.

sections.heading: Lagrange multipliers: setting up the system

questions.q: Set up the Lagrange multiplier equations to optimize $f(x,y)=xy$ subject to $g(x,y)=x+y-10=0$.
questions.answer: $\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g$: $\langle y,x\rangle=\lambda\langle1,1\rangle \Rightarrow y=\lambda,\ x=\lambda \Rightarrow x=y$, together with the constraint $x+y=10$.

questions.q: Set up the Lagrange multiplier equations to optimize $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ subject to $g(x,y)=xy-1=0$.
questions.answer: $\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g$: $\langle2x,2y\rangle=\lambda\langle y,x\rangle \Rightarrow 2x=\lambda y$ and $2y=\lambda x$, together with the constraint $xy=1$.

questions.q: Maximize $f(x,y)=xy$ subject to $x+y=10$.
questions.answer: From the setup above, $x=y$ and $x+y=10 \Rightarrow x=y=5$. Maximum value: $f(5,5)=25$.

questions.q: Minimize $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ subject to $x+y=4$.
questions.answer: $\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g$: $\langle2x,2y\rangle=\lambda\langle1,1\rangle \Rightarrow x=y$. With $x+y=4$: $x=y=2$. Minimum value: $f(2,2)=8$.

questions.q: Solve the system from the earlier setup question to minimize $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ subject to $xy=1$.
questions.answer: From $2x=\lambda y$ and $2y=\lambda x$: multiplying, $4xy=\lambda^2 xy$, and since $xy=1\ne0$, $\lambda^2=4 \Rightarrow \lambda=\pm2$. If $\lambda=2$: $2x=2y \Rightarrow x=y$; with $xy=1$: $x=y=1$ or $x=y=-1$. Both give $f=1+1=2$. (If $\lambda=-2$: $x=-y$, but then $xy=-x^2<0\ne1$, no real solution.) Minimum value: $f=2$, at $(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1)$.

questions.q: Find the point on the line $x+y=6$ closest to the origin, using Lagrange multipliers on $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$.
questions.answer: $\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g$: $\langle2x,2y\rangle=\lambda\langle1,1\rangle \Rightarrow x=y$. With $x+y=6$: $x=y=3$. Closest point: $(3,3)$, at distance $\sqrt{9+9}=3\sqrt{2}$.

questions.q: A rectangle has perimeter $20$. Use Lagrange multipliers to maximize its area $A=xy$ subject to the constraint $2x+2y=20$ (i.e., $x+y=10$).
questions.answer: This matches the very first Lagrange problem above: $x=y=5$, giving maximum area $A=25$ — a square, as expected.

questions.q: Set up (but do not fully solve) the Lagrange multiplier equations to minimize $f(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2+z^2$ subject to $g(x,y,z)=x+y+z-6=0$.
questions.answer: $\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g$: $\langle2x,2y,2z\rangle=\lambda\langle1,1,1\rangle \Rightarrow 2x=2y=2z=\lambda$, so $x=y=z$, together with $x+y+z=6$.

questions.q: Solve the three-variable problem set up above.
questions.answer: From $x=y=z$ and $x+y+z=6$: $3x=6 \Rightarrow x=y=z=2$. Minimum value: $f(2,2,2)=4+4+4=12$.

questions.q: In the rectangle-area problem above ($x=y=5$, $\lambda=5$), briefly explain what $\lambda$ represents in economic/physical terms: the approximate change in the optimal value of $f$ per unit increase in the constraint constant.
questions.answer: $\lambda$ approximates $\dfrac{dA^*}{dc}$, where $A^*$ is the optimal (maximum) area and $c$ is the perimeter constant (here $c=20$, giving $x+y=10$). So increasing the perimeter by $1$ unit (from $20$ to $21$) would increase the maximum enclosed area by approximately $\lambda=5$.

sections.heading: Optimization on a closed region (global extrema)

questions.q: Explain the general procedure for finding the global maximum and minimum of a continuous $f(x,y)$ on a closed, bounded region $R$.
questions.answer: (1) Find all critical points of $f$ in the interior of $R$ and evaluate $f$ there. (2) Find the extrema of $f$ restricted to the boundary of $R$ (often via substitution or Lagrange multipliers) and evaluate $f$ at those boundary extrema, including corners. (3) Compare all these values — the largest is the global maximum, the smallest is the global minimum (guaranteed to exist by the Extreme Value Theorem for continuous $f$ on a closed, bounded region).

questions.q: Find the only interior critical point of $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2-2x$ on the closed disk $x^2+y^2\leq4$, and evaluate $f$ there.
questions.answer: $f_x=2x-2=0 \Rightarrow x=1$. $f_y=2y=0 \Rightarrow y=0$. Critical point $(1,0)$, which lies inside the disk since $1^2+0^2=1<4$. $f(1,0)=1+0-2=-1$.

questions.q: For the same $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2-2x$ on $x^2+y^2\leq4$, find the maximum of $f$ on the boundary circle $x^2+y^2=4$ using Lagrange multipliers.
questions.answer: $\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g$ with $g=x^2+y^2-4$: $\langle2x-2,2y\rangle=\lambda\langle2x,2y\rangle$. From the $y$-component: $2y=2\lambda y \Rightarrow y=0$ or $\lambda=1$. If $y=0$: $x^2=4 \Rightarrow x=\pm2$, giving $f(2,0)=4-4=0$ and $f(-2,0)=4+4=8$. If $\lambda=1$: $2x-2=2x \Rightarrow -2=0$, impossible. So on the boundary, the maximum is $f(-2,0)=8$.

questions.q: Combine the results above to state the global maximum and minimum of $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2-2x$ on the disk $x^2+y^2\leq4$.
questions.answer: Candidates: interior critical point $f(1,0)=-1$; boundary values $f(2,0)=0$ and $f(-2,0)=8$. Global minimum: $-1$ at $(1,0)$. Global maximum: $8$ at $(-2,0)$.

questions.q: Explain why the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees this problem has a global max and min, and why that guarantee would fail on the OPEN disk $x^2+y^2<4$.
questions.answer: The Extreme Value Theorem requires the region to be closed and bounded; the closed disk $x^2+y^2\leq4$ satisfies both. The open disk $x^2+y^2<4$ is bounded but not closed (it excludes its boundary circle), so a continuous function need not attain a maximum or minimum on it — e.g., $f$ could approach its boundary supremum without ever reaching it inside the open region.

questions.q: Find the global maximum and minimum of $f(x,y)=xy$ on the closed square $-1\leq x\leq1$, $-1\leq y\leq1$, by checking the interior critical point and all four corners (the boundary edges of a square are easiest checked at their endpoints for a bilinear function like $xy$).
